Lesson No. 144: Explanation of the Verses 1 to 24

Verses 1 to 2: "O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing."

With the force of its words, this is a frightening opening to the discourse. A person becomes so fearful that his heart trembles. All of mankind is addressed in a loud and forceful voice: "O people!! O mankind! Fear Allah, fear Allah," "Fear your Lord." "Of what day do We warn you?" "Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing" (22:1). The details of this convulsion and of this great and terrifying thing are not given here, and this increases its terror. It is a convulsion! It is tremendous! It is frightening! It cannot be described in words. Simply fear it, just as a person who says "Run, run!" first and only afterwards gives the reason.

When the details that follow are given briefly, the terror of this convulsion increases greatly. It is a scene in which nursing mothers leave their infants and flee here and there, seeing nothing and perceiving nothing; it is all running. In that terror and rush, every pregnant woman's pregnancy is miscarried, and some lie here and some there. People appear to be stupefied, yet in reality they will not be intoxicated. Their dazed gaze and staggering steps indicate intoxication, but in truth they are distraught. This scene is filled with movement and chaos. The waves of people rush from one side to the other, yet no one knows why there is such a flood of humanity. Human thought falls behind this scene described in the Qur'anic manner, and the eye of imagination cannot reach the last part of this turbulent flood of people. It is so terrifying a scene that its size and magnitude cannot be estimated. A woman, even in fire, keeps her child clasped to her breast, but how tremendous and terrifying a scene it will be when women cast their children away from their breasts, and all pregnant women abort their pregnancies, and people are in a state of stupefaction. The real point is:

"But the punishment of Allah is severe" (22:2). At the thought of it, hair stands on end, while they are seeing it with their own eyes... This is the beginning of the Surah, convulsive and frightening!

Despite such scenes, some people are so hard-hearted that they speak foolish things about Allah, and the fear of Allah is not in their hearts.

Discussion about Allah: whether it concerns the existence of Allah, His oneness, His power, His knowledge, or any of His attributes, and bearing in mind the terrifying scenes the human being must face and the dreadful stations he must pass through, such a discussion appears strange and bold coming from any intelligent person. This picture alone is enough to terrify a sinful and error-prone servant.

If only those who speak about Allah would speak with knowledge (ʿilm), recognition (maʿrifah) and certainty (yaqin), and speak with insight (ʿala wajh al-basirah). But they exceed their limits without knowledge, and this kind of debate and contention arises from obedience to the accursed Shaytan. Among people there are always such individuals, who speak such things while following the desires of their own selves.

﴿And he follows every rebellious devil﴾ (22:3), who is disobedient, opposed to the truth, and arrogant.

﴿For it has been decreed concerning him that whoever takes him as an ally, he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾ (22:4). So the inevitable outcome of befriending him is that he will cast his friend into Hell. Why, then, does any intelligent person, seeing and understanding this, make friends with such a person and take guidance from him?

The state of people is that they regard resurrection after death with doubt, and even in the tremor of the Final Hour they are in doubt. They will find countless proofs of the Resurrection. But the misfortune of people is that they pass over these proofs with heedlessness.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 22, verses 5–6:

What is the reality of resurrection after death? It is simply the infusion of life again into the parts of the body. By human reckoning, this is easier than the original creation; but if a person regards it as difficult, then in relation to Allah it is very easy. It is no difficult matter. To re-create, Allah need only will it, saying (Kun), that is, "Be," and it will be.

﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ The manner of the Qur'an's discourse is that it speaks in accordance with human thought and conjecture, in accordance with people's modes of reasoning and their capacity for perception. Thus the Qur'an invites them to reflect upon the universe spread out before them and visible to them. Let them constantly observe those well-known and visible events that pass before their eyes at all times. If one reflects deeply upon the events of day and night that pass before their eyes, all those events would appear to a person as a great miracle, provided that they study them deeply with an open heart and a seeing eye. But the state of people is that they pass over these events and scenes as deaf and dumb, or these events and scenes pass by them, and people receive no warning. The question, and the greatest question, is: what is man himself? Where has he come from? How did he come? And through what stages has he passed?

﴿Indeed, We created you from dust﴾ (22:5). Man is a son of this dust. From this dust he has been formed; this body of his has been moulded from this dust; it is from dust that the growth of his life proceeds. All the elements that are in his body exist within the earth. Only one element is not in the dust, namely "life," that is, the soul. This is a matter of the Lord's command, and our knowledge concerning it is still limited. Because of this soul he has become separated from the dust, yet in origin he is indeed dust. His physical structure, his nourishment, and all the components of his body are from the dust.

The question is how, then, a difference arose between dust and man. Where is the dust and where is man? Dust is merely simple particles, but man, after creation, is also "fashioned" (fasawwahā). This man is both an agent and one who receives the effect of action; he influences and is influenced. His feet are upon the earth, and his flight is toward the heavens. By his thought he produces creations beyond matter, and within matter too he has his creations.

Is it not a great miracle and a great transformation that Allah has made a human being from dust? For such a Creator, to gather again this human matter is what difficulty could there be? A strange creature, made from matter.

﴿Then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, partly formed and partly unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We cause to remain in the wombs whom We will for an appointed term, then We bring you forth as infants﴾ (22:5). [This is what We are explaining] so that the truth may become clear to you. Consider these simple elements of dust, then consider the semen, which is in the form of living cells of the earth. How great the change has come about! Within it lies that great secret, namely the secret of life, a secret concerning which mankind to this day has not been able to acquire any worthwhile knowledge. Billions of years have passed. Man is striving to find out what the soul is and what life is. During these billions of years, billions of living cells are formed in every drop of semen, but we are incapable even of observing these cells, let alone understanding their creation, even if man raises his gaze and grasps at the impossible.

Then how does this drop become a clot, how does it take the form of a clot of blood? Then how does this blood come to take the form of flesh, and how does this flesh take on the form of a human being? What is semen? It is the water of the male. A single drop of semen contains hundreds of thousands of spermatozoa. Out of these thousands and millions of creatures, only one creature enters the ovum of the woman, which is in the womb. It unites with it, and clings to the wall of the womb. In that ovum, which is as small as a point, and which becomes attached to the walls of the mother's womb, this tiny swimming creature in the semen becomes attached, indeed enters inside that ovum. This act takes place according to an automatic system. Allah has placed acceptance in these two things. In that point Allah has deposited all the human qualities and habits. All the characteristics of the coming human being: what his weight will be, how tall he will be, what his build will be, how much corpulence he will have, whether he will be beautiful or ugly, healthy or sick. Within it are deposited a person's nervous characteristics, intellectual capacities, and psychological conditions. His inclinations, emotions, and tendencies, toward goodness or toward evil, exist within that small creature itself.

Who could imagine that within the union of the ovum suspended in the womb and this small creature, all this exists, and that within this point, visible only through a microscope, there is a complete human being whose bodily structure is itself intricate? So much so that in the world no single person is a perfect likeness of another, and from Adam until today no two persons are completely alike.

Now this point changes from a clot to a lump of flesh. It is a lump of thickened blood, having no shape or form. Then this lump of flesh again takes on a form, and it becomes a framework of bones over which flesh is laid. If it is destined to be born, it is born; otherwise the womb expels it, if Allah has not decreed for it a coming into the world as a human being.

﴿That We may make clear to you﴾. Between the lump of flesh and the infant, the Qur'an makes an interjected remark, so that We may tell you what marvellous capacities the power of Allah has placed within this lump of blood. This is the highly effective style of expression of the Qur'an. Then comes the state of the foetus in the womb.

﴿And We cause to remain in the wombs whom We will for an appointed term﴾ (22:5). Those foetuses which Allah wills to complete remain in the womb until their appointed time of delivery.

﴿Then We bring you forth as infants﴾ (22:5). Look at the suspended drop of semen, and look at the newborn child; how great is the difference between the two.

If one considers this period, it is very short, usually only nine months; and if one looks at the suspended drop of semen and looks at the newborn child, there is a very great difference between the two. The drop of semen cannot even be seen without a microscope, whereas the child is a highly intricate, complete creature with limbs and organs, with its own features, its own qualities and capacities, and its emotions and inclinations. This difference is so great that no sensible, intelligent, and reflective person can proceed without repeatedly contemplating it and acknowledging the power of Allah.

After this, the Qur'an moves on a little further with the circumstances of the newborn. This child sees light and leaves that hidden place within which it passed this miraculous journey, and where it remained out of sight.

﴿Then you are brought forth, that you may reach your maturity﴾ (22:5), and that you may complete your bodily structure, that your intellect may reach maturity, and that you may become a psychologically developed person. At this point it is worth reflecting how many stages lie between a newborn baby and a fully grown, strong adult. The distance between them is immense, far greater than the distance of ages. Yet the hand of power has carried all these distances through. The hand of power has bestowed upon this child all human attributes, and the suspended drop of semen, which consisted of a worthless water, has now become a complete human being.

Then:

﴿And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that after knowing he knows nothing﴾ (22:5). Whoever is taken away, that is, dies early, arrives at that end which is the final end of every living thing. Whoever is returned to the most wretched age, it is a matter for our reflection that after knowledge, understanding, perception and perfection, he again becomes a child. His emotions, impressions and memory become like those of children; he cannot hold anything in his hand. His memory vanishes; he remembers nothing. Thus a child looks upon every incident as a single isolated event; he cannot see the connection between two events. Then he keeps asking about everything again and again, and cannot reach any conclusion, because by the time he sees the final event he has forgotten the earlier links.

﴿So that after knowing he knows nothing﴾ (22:5). Those sciences in which he was once a great expert slip out of his grasp, and at one time he even used to debate concerning the Being and attributes of Allah.

After this, moving beyond the creation and upbringing of human beings, the discussion turns to the creative process of animals and plants within the earth.

﴿And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and puts forth every lovely kind of growth﴾ (22:5). The earth lies dry, then where We send down rain upon it, it suddenly stirs, swells, and produces every kind of pleasing vegetation.

Lifelessness is a stage between death and life. Before rain or water reaches it, the earth is in a state of lifelessness. Water is a major element in animals and plants; when it descends, this earth ﴿stirs and swells﴾ (22:5). This is a remarkable motion, which the Qur'an has recorded, before it could be observed by scientific instruments. When dry earth receives water, it moves, it quivers, it drinks, it swells. After this, plants sprout forth from it. ﴿Every lovely kind of pair﴾ (22:5): it begins to put forth pairs of every kind of pleasing vegetation. Nothing is more beautiful a scene than when the earth, from a state of stillness and death, is once again filled with life and blooms with verdure.

The Qur'an, in a single verse, creates a link between all living things: human beings, animals and plants. It directs people's thought and vision to the fact that there is a profound connection among these things, and what that connection is. This kinship is evidence that the true cause of life is one: that one will which manifests it in every place. About the earth, plants, animals and humans, all of them, this verse says:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 22, verse 7:

﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ ... ﴿and that He will raise up those who are in the graves﴾ (7)

This matter, namely the creation of man from earth, then the embryo passing through the various stages mentioned above, then the child passing through the various stages of life, then the dry and dead earth being brought to life after rain, all these affairs prove that Allah is the Truth. This is because these matters show that the law of nature which the Creator of the universe has established for this world is true. It does not change, and the orderly progression of life, step by step, is proof that the will of one Single Creator and Governor is at work in this universe. In other words, there is a deep connection between the laws of nature that run through life and the entire universe, and the truth of Allah.

﴿And that He brings the dead to life﴾ (22:6) means: just as He first created man from the earth, it is not difficult for Him to give life again to that same earth; that is, to bring the dead back to life.

﴿And that Allah will raise up those who are in the graves﴾ (22:8) means: so that they may reach the end they deserve, for the wisdom of the design and the wisdom of the creation of this universe require that the dead be raised up.

These various stages through which the embryo passes, then those through which a child passes, and the moment it opens its eyes, all these stages prove that the governing will which does all these things will certainly carry this human being out of his present condition and bring him to the abode of perfection. In the life of this earth, man does not reach perfection, because he stands still at a certain point and then begins to decline.

﴿So that after knowing he may know nothing﴾ means: in its light, another world and another life are necessary for man in which he may attain perfection.

The creation of man, of animals and of plants, and their stages of development, indicate that the One who created them is also able to recreate them. Secondly, He will in practice raise them up and take them to another world so that they may reach the degree of perfection there. Thus the principle of creation and the law of resurrection after death come together, and then the reckoning in the Hereafter also becomes their natural end, and from all these matters the proof of the Creator and Governor is also obtained, whose hand is at work in all these affairs.

Despite these countless proofs, some people still dispute about Allah.

Among people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book. (Note: the passage's opening verse text is given in the source as a fragment; translating the commentary as it stands:)

It seems strange and extremely wicked to speak about Allah in dispute even after these proofs have been presented. Moreover, those who engage in such disputation are not people of knowledge. They have no argument. They have no special insight in this field. And they have not brought any Book that enlightens the intellect, clarifies the truth, and points to a certain path.

Here there is also a particular depiction of such people who have stiffened their necks out of arrogance.

﴿Thāniya ʿiṭfih﴾ (22:9) "turning aside (with his neck)". His speech is not backed by proof; rather, he speaks with arrogance. He is a proud tyrant.

﴿Liyuḍilla ʿan sabīlillāh﴾ (22:9) "so that he may lead others astray from the path of Allah." Such people are not content merely to be astray themselves; they also lead others astray.

Therefore such arrogance, harsh greatness, and haughtiness must be broken, so that it is shattered to pieces.

﴿Lahu fid-dunyā khizy﴾ (22:9) "For him there is disgrace in this world." Disgrace and humiliation are the exact opposite of pride and arrogance. It is Allah's established law that He breaks the pride of these deniers, the haughty, those who go astray, and those who lead others astray, though perhaps after a period of time. Indeed, Allah grants such people respite so that when their downfall comes, they are greatly humiliated and abased, and this humiliation has a greater impact upon them. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 22, verses 11–13:

﴿And among mankind is he who worships Allah on the verge (of faith); if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾ (22:11)

﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the far-straying error.﴾ (22:12–13 in part)

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Wretched is the protector, and wretched is the companion.﴾ (22:13)

Belief and ideology are the capital of a believer's life, and his life stands upon them. In the believer's environment, the waves of agitation in the sea of life come and go, and fierce stormy winds keep blowing, yet the believer grips a rock firmly in the middle of the sea and remains steadfast. Around him, support after support falls away, but he has grasped a firm support, and his feet are not shaken.

In the life of a true believer, ideology has this value, and therefore he must stand firm upon it. He must hold it tightly. He must be certain that this creed is the true creed. There should be no wavering within him about it, and he should not seek any gift or reward in return for it, because for the believer his ideology is his gain. This creed and ideology is his refuge; it is his support. It is his recompense, because through it his heart has received light, he has come onto the path of guidance, and he has found tranquility in it.

When a believer is in the refuge of the Islamic ideology of life and sees that around him, among his environment, people are wandering aimlessly, like fallen leaves of a tree, sometimes the autumn wind carries them this way and sometimes that way, and the whirlwinds of storms scatter them about, and they are the victims of severe anguish and restlessness, while he remains established and content in his ideology. He is steadfast, there is calm and composure in his movements, and he works night and day seeking the pleasure of Allah.

The people being spoken of here are those who trade in ideologies, who carry their faith and conscience to the marketplace.

"If good befalls him, he is content with it" (22:11): and he says that faith is nothing but good. Now this person earns profit from that ideology; he milks the udders, sows and reaps, and his trade runs in the market, and he keeps it going.

"And if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face; he has lost this world and the Hereafter" (22:11): he has lost this world in that a minor affliction came to him and he could not endure it; he could not remain firm in his position. In hard times he did not turn to Allah, and he has lost the Hereafter in that he first abandoned faith and ideology and chose the path of misguidance instead of the path of guidance.

Here the Qur'an says about such people that they worship Allah from the edge. They do not hold firmly to the Islamic ideology of life, they are not steadfast in the work of da'wah, and their position is described such that they stand in ideological stance at a place where a slight jolt would make them fall. Merely a little difficulty comes and they run away. Their standing on the edge was for the very purpose that escape would be easy.

The fact is that measuring things by profit and loss is the nature of commercial dealings. In ideologies, the standard of worldly gain and loss does not apply. In ideologies one should see what is truth and what is falsehood. One should support the truth, because in ideology the truth is that in which a worker is satisfied with his movement through insight. Its profit is simply that a person finds the truth. A person is satisfied with it in his heart, and therein he finds inner peace and comfort. This is indeed the goal of a believer. Upon this, a true believer seeks no external reward.

A true believer worships his Lord because He has guided him. He worships because faith has been made beloved to him, and he loves faith and ideology. If some worldly benefit also comes to him, that is good as a recompense; it will be a reward for his servitude and faith.

A true believer does not test his God from the standpoint of profit and loss. When he accepts Islam, he accepts every trial along with it. He is content that his Lord may test him in whatever way He wishes; he is ready. Whether there is prosperity and his Lord tests him in it, or there is adversity and his Lord tests him in that, he is content in every state. This is not a transaction like the sale between a seller and a buyer in the market, in which he constantly calculates profit and loss. Rather, here it is a matter of submitting before the Creator. The authority belongs to Allah to do as He wills, because it is Allah who created the believer.

Whoever turns away from his faith and ideology and goes back on his heels falls into a loss about which there is no doubt.

﴿That is the manifest loss﴾ (22:11): the tranquility of his life is gone, his confidence is gone, his peace is gone, and he is deprived of the pleasure of Allah. Along with the loss of health, wealth and children, the loss of the Hereafter is an enormous loss. Alongside this loss in the world, Allah tests His servants: through their trust, their reliance, their patience, their sincerity, and their resolve, He tests whether they are ready to accept the decrees of Allah's destiny or not. And the loss of the Hereafter is a very great loss, for he is deprived of the eternal blessings of the Hereafter. He is deprived of Allah's good pleasure and nearness to Allah. This is the manifest loss.

But this person who worships Allah from the edge, where will he go? Far from Allah, where will he go?

﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which can neither harm him nor benefit him﴾ (22:12): he worships idols, or he worships some personality, as was the custom in the first Jahiliyyah. In the modern age he will run after some party, some dictator, or some interest, as is the form of modern jahiliyyah. The fact is that whenever people have ceased to call upon Allah alone, and ceased to follow His pleasure and His system of life, what has been their end? Such people, deprived of focus and unity, become scattered.

﴿That is the far-straying error﴾ (22:13): he calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit, that is, idols, or Satan, or shrines. The harm of all these things is nearer and the benefit is far. The harm is that disorder arises in the human heart and mind; delusion, humiliation and backwardness fall to his lot, and the loss of the Hereafter is very great indeed.

﴿Wretched is the protector﴾ (22:13): that is, one who can neither benefit nor harm.

﴿And wretched is the companion﴾ (22:13): that is, this companion through whom this loss is suffered. In it are included idols and also human beings, because some people also make humans into gods or god-like beings. In every age such humans have been gods, and the rewards for believers are very great and precious. Even if a Muslim stakes everything in the world, the reward kept for them is still greater and more precious.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 22, verse 15:

من کان یظن ……ما یغیظ (15)

This is an extremely vivid scene, in which the psychological rage and anger of a person is displayed, along with the actions that such a person takes in circumstances of this kind. Situations are presented in embodied form in which a person's anger and restlessness reach their peak. A person who is beset by difficulties and has no connection with the Lord, the Exalted, is one who, at the time of calamity, becomes despairing from every direction. He sees no ray of hope anywhere, and finds no window through which a breeze of relief might come from any side. Such a person is constrained by tightness of breath and inner anguish to an unbearable degree, and in this state of despair, grief, distress and restlessness torment him further. Thus the Qur'an says to such a person that if he is so distressed, let him reach the heavens by means of a rope and hang himself from that rope. Either he will commit suicide and fall down, or his life will leave him by means of it. Then let him see whether, through such measures, he can extricate himself from that wretched state.

It is worth remembering that continuous afflictions can be endured in only one way: when a person has hope in the mercy of God. Calamities and difficulties can be removed only when a person turns his attention to Allah. The sole way to overcome trials and difficulties and to emerge from them is that a person seeks help from Allah alone. Every action of a despairing person causes greater despair and greater calamities, and when a afflicted person becomes despairing, calamity begins to oppress him all the more. Therefore I invite all those who are being ground in the mill of trials and afflictions to seek help from Allah. This is the only path by which they can find peace, and upon them the breeze of Allah's mercy can blow.

…………

وکذلک ……من یرید (16)

The introduction and description of these groups has already passed. Here their mention is in relation to the principle that Allah guides whomever He wills, and that He also knows who is upon guidance and who is upon misguidance. If people are running after their own thoughts, their desires and their personal inclinations, then let them keep running. This entire universe, with its nature, is obedient to the laws of Allah's power and prostrates before Him. If there is any disobedient creature, it is the human being.

Alam tara … ma yashā' (18)

When a person reflects on this verse, he sees a vast multitude of God's creatures: those that are visible and those that are not, in the heavens and among the celestial bodies, things that are seen and things that are not seen, and those that become visible only with the help of extremely sensitive instruments. Countless mountains, trees, creatures that crawl upon the earth, birds and beasts, in short, this flood of divine creation, prostrates itself before Allah. It turns its attention to Allah alone, turning to Him with the utmost unity and harmony. But if there is any disobedient one among this creation, it is the human being. He is the only creature that disobeys in a bold manner.

Wa kathīrun mina l-nās wa kathīrun ḥaqqa ʿalayhi l-ʿadhāb (22:18): "Many people, and many others also, have become deserving of punishment." That is, in this creation which bows and prostrates itself to Allah, the human being alone appears as a strange thing.

Therefore it is decreed that whoever has become deserving of My punishment, that is, whoever has become worthy of it, has become humiliated.

Wa man yuhini llāhu fa-mā lahu min mukrim (22:18): "And whomever Allah humiliates, there is no one to honour him." Hence, honour is that which Allah grants. Power is that which Allah has given. Whoever bows before anyone other than Allah has been humiliated and disgraced.

Now, one of the scenes of the Day of Judgement, in which the honouring by Allah and the humiliation by Allah appear plainly, as if all of this were present before our eyes on a screen, let us look at the screen.

This is a strange, frightening scene full of cries and commotion, brimming with movement. The Quran's finest manner of expression creates within the mind this long imaginative vision so that it appears clearly, as if on a screen. This scene repeatedly seizes the hem of the imagination, and the imagination cannot shake itself free of it.

Garments of fire are being cut, each one tailored for each individual. Scalding hot water is being poured over the heads of the people of the Fire. As soon as the water is poured, their skins, and indeed the insides of their bodies, dissolve and rot. There are iron whips, heated in the fire. The punishment grows ever harsher, beyond the limit of endurance. People panic, run about, and make their futile attempts to escape from Hell, but they are forcefully pushed back inside again. They are harshly rebuked.

﴿وَذُوقُوا عَذَابَ الْحَرِيقِ﴾ (22:22) "Taste the punishment of burning." The imagination keeps repeating all these scenes, until, amid the attempts to flee and the harsh driving of people back into Hell, the same image keeps running through the mind, when suddenly another scene appears: the scene of the other party of the two companions. We have just seen the condition of one party; now the people of Paradise are drawn upon the screen. There are gardens beneath which rivers flow. Their garments are being stitched not from fire but from silk. Along with these garments, there are ornaments to beautify their bodies: bracelets of gold and pearls. Then there are garment upon garment, and they are people of gracious speech. They are upon the straight path of Allah, the Exalted. Their speech is neither harsh nor is their path burdensome. Lesson No. 145: At a Glance

The previous lesson ended with the point that people are divided into two groups regarding the Divine Being, and with what the end of the disbelievers will be on the Day of Judgment and how the believers will fare. In this connection, the conduct the disbelievers have adopted in this world is now discussed: they have begun to prevent people from visiting the Sacred Mosque (Masjid al-Haram). In Makkah they struggled ceaselessly to block the path of the Islamic call, but when this movement shifted to Madinah, they prevented the Muslims from visiting the Haram.

In this regard, it is explained what purposes Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had in mind when he built this Haram, and for what purposes, after its construction, he proclaimed among the people that they should come freely to visit this Haram. The building of this House was itself founded upon the belief in Tawhid (the Oneness of God). It was a House of Tawhid, and there is no justification at all for associating partners with God in it. Furthermore, this House was for all of mankind, whether one resides in it or comes to it from outside. It is a common place for all. No one can prevent anyone from entering it, and no one can become its owner.

Here some of the rites of pilgrimage and visitation are also described, and it is also made clear what feeling of God-fearing and connection with God lies behind them. Finally, it is explained that no one is permitted to commit any oppression against anyone within the Haram, especially those who use the Haram for purposes for which it was not built. Such people have no right at all to be its custodians. Whoever rises to free this Haram and fulfils the requirements of this mission, the help of Allah will be with him. This will not be aggression, but rather a defence against those who lay hands upon the purposes of the Haram.

Lesson No. 145: Explanation of the Verses

25 to 41

Inna alladhina ... alimin (25)

This was the conduct of the polytheist Quraysh: they prevented people from the religion of Allah and from the Sacred Mosque, although the Sacred Mosque was built for the people, whether they were its residents or those who came from outside to visit it. The religion of Allah is the means through which a human being can reach Allah. Then, for people, it is a system of life according to which they are to conduct their lives, because it is the methodology of their life. The Quraysh used to prevent people from the religion of Islam and also from the Sacred Mosque. They even prevented the Muslims from Hajj and Umrah, although Allah had declared the Sacred Mosque a House of security and peace in which the inhabitants of Makkah and outsiders were all equal. Here no one had any distinctive position. No one could become its owner, nor could anyone acquire exclusive rights.

This is the sacred place which Allah chose first of all to be declared a peaceful territory. In this territory people would lay down their weapons, and even two persons with intense enmity between them would live here in peace. Every kind of bloodshed was forbidden here. This was not anyone's favour; rather it was a right of all mankind, and in this right all were equal.

Among the jurists there is a difference of opinion regarding whether the houses of Makkah, in which their owners do not reside, can have an owner, and, if the legitimacy of ownership is established, whether the rent of these houses may be taken. Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) holds that ownership is permissible, inheritance is permissible, and renting them out is permissible. He draws evidence from the narration of Hadrat Umar ibn al-Khattab, who purchased a house in Makkah from Safwan ibn Umayyah for four thousand dirhams and made a prison from it. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh holds that its houses cannot be inherited and cannot be rented out. He says that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Hadrat Abu Bakr and Hadrat Umar passed away at a time when the land of Makkah was called shared land (shamilat); whoever needed it would live in it, and whoever had more than he needed would settle another person in it. Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Mujahid, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Umar, that he said the houses of Makkah may not be sold, nor is it permissible to take their rent. He also narrated from Ibn Juraij that Ata used to forbid renting out houses within the Haram, and he told me that Hadrat Umar ibn al-Khattab used to forbid fixing doors to the houses of Makkah so that pilgrims could stay in their courtyards. Suhayl ibn Amr was the first to fix a door. Hadrat Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote to him regarding this matter. In reply he said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am a trader, so I have fixed two doors so that I may keep my riding animals here." Upon this he said: "You are permitted to do so." In a narration of Mujahid it is reported that Hadrat Umar said to the people of Makkah: "Do not fix gates in front of your houses, so that a pilgrim may alight wherever he wishes." Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal adopted a middle position: that ownership and inheritance apply to them, but renting them out is not permissible. In this way he has reconciled the evidences.

Thus Islam, in contrast to all other religions, first declared a region to be a House of security, and it declared it to be a city of all mankind, and it forbade ownership and other boundary-making within it. Accordingly, the Holy Qur'an threatens whoever introduces crookedness into this clear and straight method, that he will be given a severe punishment.

"Whoever intends therein deviation or wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment" (22:25). This punishment is for the one who intends and then commits wrongdoing; and whoever commits oppression after intending it, his punishment will be even greater. The announcement of punishment merely for intention is for the sake of great emphasis. This is an extremely subtle expression of the Holy Qur'an.

Furthermore, proof of the profound emphatic style of the Holy Qur'an is also found in the fact that in this sentence the predicate of "inna" is not mentioned:

"Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque" (22:25).

Here there is no mention of what the ruling about these disbelievers is, what their end will be, or what punishment they will receive. From the mention of their disbelief itself it becomes known what their recompense is, since they are here barring people and also barring the path of Islam.

Now the discourse turns to the construction and history of that House, over which the polytheists have taken control. In it these people worship idols, and they deprive the people of Tawhid of the right of visitation merely because they are free from shirk. It is explained how, in accordance with the instructions and commands of the Lord, this Ka'bah came into existence: it was built precisely so that it would be the foundation of Tawhid, that its use would be that Allah alone is worshipped in it, and that it would be specifically for both its resident people and its visitors.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 22, verse 26–29:

From the first day this house was built for Tawhid. Allah Himself indicated to Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) the place for it, and gave him the authority to build it on that foundation.

*Anlā tushrik bī shay'an* (22:25) "Do not associate anything with Me," because this is only the House of Allah. No one else has any share in it apart from Allah, and keep it pure for the pilgrims and for those who establish prayer.

*Wa-ṭahhir baytiya lil-ṭā'ifīna wal-qā'imīna war-rukkaʿi's-sujūd* (22:25) "And purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand, bow, and prostrate." These are the people for whom the House of Allah was built. It was not built for the polytheists who worship others besides Allah.

After this, Allah commanded Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him), the builder of the House of Allah, that once this house was built for these purposes, he should proclaim among the people that they should come for Hajj, and Allah promised that the people would respond to this proclamation. Therefore, they will come in rows, on camels and on foot, from far-off places, so far that their camels will become lean due to the distance of the journey.

The promise Allah made to Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is being fulfilled even today and will be fulfilled tomorrow as well. To this day, people's hearts are attached to the Kaʿbah. People's hearts throb for the sight of the House of Allah and for tawaf. Whoever is wealthy, has the means for the journey, and has the facility of transport, comes on transport, on the most modern transport, and whoever has only feet comes on foot to visit this house. Millions of people from far-off regions, from the deep valleys and even from the heights of the sky, every year come pouring in rows upon rows. Thousands of years have passed, and the proclamation of Hazrat Ibrahim and the promise of Allah are still being fulfilled.

Here, some of the rites of Hajj and some of its purposes are also mentioned:

*Li-yashhadū manāfiʿa lahum … bil-bayti al-ʿatīq* (22:28–29) "So that they may witness the benefits made available for them, and mention the name of Allah on known days over the animals He has provided for them. Then eat from them and feed the distressed poor. Then let them end their untidiness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the ancient House."

What are the benefits that pilgrims witness? Hajj is in reality a global gathering and fair; it is a season of trade and a season of worship. It is a global gathering in which Muslims from across the world come to know one another. All Muslims cooperate with one another, and unity is created among them.

It is a form of worship in which both this world and the Hereafter come together, and it is in reality also a visit to the ancient monuments of the Islamic worldview. For people who bring travel goods and products, it is an excellent marketplace. You see that the food supplies and fruits of the world come to this House from the surrounding lands and are brought there. Pilgrims are drawn from all regions, and along with them come the good things and good conduct of their lands, and then this fragrance spreads throughout the Islamic world. All these people gather at the Sacred House in different seasons, and also gather in a single season, so it is in effect a commercial marketplace and also a trade fair.

Furthermore, Hajj is a global gathering of worship in which spiritual purification takes place. The human soul feels that in this honoured House of Allah it has come closer to Allah. This soul longs for the Kaʿbah, and the spiritual memories associated with the Kaʿbah, and the souls of the revered personalities connected with it, are felt to be circling here: the souls of recent times and the souls of distant times.

Look, this is the soul of Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him); he is leaving his beloved son Ismaʿil and his mother within the House of Allah. With a fearful and throbbing heart he turns towards the Lord, the Exalted.

*Rabbanā innī askantu … la-ʿallahum yashkurūn* (14:37) "Our Lord, I have settled a part of my offspring in an uncultivated valley near Your sacred House. Our Lord, I have done this so that they may establish prayer here. So make the hearts of people incline towards them, and provide them with fruits to eat, so that perhaps they may be grateful."

Then the image of Hazrat Hajar comes to mind: for herself and for her infant child, in the scorching heat searching for water, she is running around the House of Allah. Then she is seen running between Safa and Marwah; she is exhausted from thirst, worn out and tired, and fears for her child's life. When she returns for the seventh time, she is broken by despair. She sees before the beautiful child a spring of clear water gushing forth. This is the spring of Zamzam. In the desert of dryness and despair, it is a spring of the mercy of Allah.

Then the image of Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) appears in the imagination. He sees in a dream that he is slaughtering Hazrat Ismaʿil. He immediately prepares to sacrifice his beloved child. Without the slightest hesitation for a moment, he attains the lofty station of believing obedience.

*Qāla yā bunayya innī arā fī al-manāmi annī adhbaḥuka fa-unẓur māḏā tara* "He said, 'O my son, I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you; what do you think?'" Hazrat Ismaʿil (peace be upon him) also answers with great obedience:

*Yā abati if'al mā tu'mar, satajidunī in shā' Allāh min aṣ-ṣābirīn* "Father, do what you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient." When both of them are prepared, the mercy of Allah is stirred, and the ransom in exchange for this sacrifice is accepted.

*Wa-nādaynāhu an yā Ibrāhīm (103) qad ṣaddaqta al-ru'yā; innā kadhālika najzī al-muḥsinīn (105) inna hādhā lahuwa al-balā'u al-mubīn (106) wa-fadaynāhu bi-dhibḥin ʿaẓīm (108)* (37:103–108) "And We called out to him, 'O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision.' Thus do We reward the good-doers. Indeed, this was a clear trial. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice." And We freed that child by giving a great sacrifice as ransom.

Then Hazrat Ibrahim and Ismaʿil (peace be upon them both) are seen raising the foundations of the Kaʿbah, making supplication with great humility and submission.

*Rabbanā taqabbal minnā … ar-raḥīm (128)* "Our Lord, accept this service from us; You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. Our Lord, make us both Muslims to You, and from our offspring raise up a community that is Muslim to You, show us our rites of worship, and forgive our shortcomings. You are the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful."

These imagined images and personalities appear before and after on the screen of the imagination, and these memories come and go, when suddenly Hazrat ʿAbd al-Muttalib appears. He makes a vow: "O Allah, if You grant me ten sons, I will dedicate the tenth son to You." The tenth son is ʿAbdullah. ʿAbd al-Muttalib wishes to fulfil his vow, and his people gather around him, and they suggest that he give a ransom. He draws arrows beside the Kaʿbah, and each time the arrow for slaughtering ʿAbdullah comes out. They keep increasing the ransom until the ransom camels reach one hundred, although the initial standard of ransom was ten she-camels. At last the arrow of ransom came out. They sacrificed one hundred camels, and the life of ʿAbdullah was spared. This was the will of Allah, because Allah was to bring forth from his loins and the womb of Aminah the highly exalted Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Thus this ransom, the great ransom, was secured by Allah for the sake of Muhammad ﷺ.

After this, many memories are still associated with this House, and on the screen of imagination new personalities keep appearing. Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ is passing through the stages of childhood, and he is walking around the House of Allah. Look, you see him lifting the Black Stone with his blessed hands and placing it in its place, so as to end the strife which threatened to cause war among the tribes. You see him praying, you see him performing tawaf, you see him delivering sermons, you see him in seclusion (iʿtikaf). Your steps are on the screen of imagination. Your image lives in hearts. It is almost that a pilgrim sees you with his eyes while he is lost and absorbed in these memories. Then before us come the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ in droves, and they walk around on this earth, performing tawaf of the House of Allah. These scenes are such that it is almost as if the ears hear and the eyes see. And beyond these memories and imaginings, Hajj is a comprehensive global gathering of Muslims. In it they come to know their true reality and their root, which in history goes back far to Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

*Millata abīkum Ibrāhīm, huwa sammākumu al-muslimīna min qablu wa-fī hādhā* "The creed of your father Ibrahim. He named you Muslims before, and in this (Qur'an)." This is the axis around which they revolve, and which has united them. It is their symbol and their banner. Under it all gather; it is an ideological symbol and an ideological banner under whose shade people of all nations, all races, all colours and all languages come together. All distinctions are erased. Here, Muslims begin to feel this strength of theirs for a limited time: the strength of the belief in Tawhid, the strength of being one community, and the strength of unity and harmony among billions of Muslims. In this gathering they feel, for a limited time, the strength they had forgotten, and they feel it in such a way that if they become one, no power in the world can stand before them, provided all these people gather under one banner upon the belief in Tawhid.

As for what Allah says, *li-yashhadū manāfiʿa lahum* (22:28) "so that they may witness their benefits which have been made available for them": every generation, according to its circumstances, according to its needs and requirements, according to its experience and demands, can derive benefits from this gathering. Allah has placed this purpose in the gathering since the time He commanded Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to call people to visit this House.

The Qur'an gives certain rites and fundamental symbols for this gathering, and in all of them there is good for all.

*Wa-yadhkurū ismallāhi fī ayyāmin maʿlūmātin ʿalā mā razaqahum min bahīmati al-anʿām* (22:28) "And that they may mention the name of Allah on known days over the cattle He has provided for them." This verse points to the sacrifice that is performed on the day of Eid and during the days of tashriq, and various sacrificial animals are slaughtered. In mentioning sacrifice, the Qur'an first commands that the name of Allah be pronounced over it, because the purpose is the worship of Allah and the attainment of His good pleasure. Here, in the act of sacrifice, the most distinctive thing mentioned is that the name of Allah should be taken over it. The meaning is that the mere slaughtering of animals is not the goal, but the real aim is to mention the name of Allah over it. (The Hanafi ruling is that sacrifice is permissible only within the two days after the Day of Nahr.)

This sacrifice is a memorial of the great slaughter of Hazrat Ismaʿil (peace be upon him). It is also a memorial of one of the miracles of Allah and one of the great acts of obedience to the command of Allah, which Hazrat Ibrahim and Hazrat Ismaʿil (peace be upon them both) left as a memorial. The benefit in this memorial is that provision of food is made for the poor and needy. The sacrificial animals are camels, cows, buffaloes, sheep and goats. (For both cows and buffaloes the Arabic word *baqar* is used.)

*Fa-kulū minhā wa-aṭʿimū al-bāʾisa al-faqīr* (22:28) "So eat from it and feed the distressed poor." From the first day this house was built for Tawhid. Allah Himself indicated to Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) the place for it, and gave him the authority to build it on that foundation.

*Anlā tushrik bī shay'an* (22:25) "Do not associate anything with Me," because this is only the House of Allah. No one else has any share in it apart from Allah, and keep it pure for the pilgrims and for those who establish prayer.

*Wa-ṭahhir baytiya lil-ṭā'ifīna wal-qā'imīna war-rukkaʿi's-sujūd* (22:25) "And purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand, bow, and prostrate." These are the people for whom the House of Allah was built. It was not built for the polytheists who worship others besides Allah.

After this, Allah commanded Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him), the builder of the House of Allah, that once this house was built for these purposes, he should proclaim among the people that they should come for Hajj, and Allah promised that the people would respond to this proclamation. Therefore, they will come in rows, on camels and on foot, from far-off places, so far that their camels will become lean due to the distance of the journey.

The promise Allah made to Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is being fulfilled even today and will be fulfilled tomorrow as well. To this day, people's hearts are attached to the Kaʿbah. People's hearts throb for the sight of the House of Allah and for tawaf. Whoever is wealthy, has the means for the journey, and has the facility of transport, comes on transport, on the most modern transport, and whoever has only feet comes on foot to visit this house. Millions of people from far-off regions, from the deep valleys and even from the heights of the sky, every year come pouring in rows upon rows. Thousands of years have passed, and the proclamation of Hazrat Ibrahim and the promise of Allah are still being fulfilled.

Here, some of the rites of Hajj and some of its purposes are also mentioned:

*Li-yashhadū manāfiʿa lahum … bil-bayti al-ʿatīq* (22:28–29) "So that they may witness the benefits made available for them, and mention the name of Allah on known days over the animals He has provided for them. Then eat from them and feed the distressed poor. Then let them end their untidiness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the ancient House."

What are the benefits that pilgrims witness? Hajj is in reality a global gathering and fair; it is a season of trade and a season of worship. It is a global gathering in which Muslims from across the world come to know one another. All Muslims cooperate with one another, and unity is created among them.

It is a form of worship in which both this world and the Hereafter come together, and it is in reality also a visit to the ancient monuments of the Islamic worldview. For people who bring travel goods and products, it is an excellent marketplace. You see that the food supplies and fruits of the world come to this House from the surrounding lands and are brought there. Pilgrims are drawn from all regions, and along with them come the good things and good conduct of their lands, and then this fragrance spreads throughout the Islamic world. All these people gather at the Sacred House in different seasons, and also gather in a single season, so it is in effect a commercial marketplace and also a trade fair.

Furthermore, Hajj is a global gathering of worship in which spiritual purification takes place. The human soul feels that in this honoured House of Allah it has come closer to Allah. This soul longs for the Kaʿbah, and the spiritual memories associated with the Kaʿbah, and the souls of the revered personalities connected with it, are felt to be circling here: the souls of recent times and the souls of distant times.

Look, this is the soul of Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him); he is leaving his beloved son Ismaʿil and his mother within the House of Allah. With a fearful and throbbing heart he turns towards the Lord, the Exalted.

*Rabbanā innī askantu … la-ʿallahum yashkurūn* (14:37) "Our Lord, I have settled a part of my offspring in an uncultivated valley near Your sacred House. Our Lord, I have done this so that they may establish prayer here. So make the hearts of people incline towards them, and provide them with fruits to eat, so that perhaps they may be grateful."

Then the image of Hazrat Hajar comes to mind: for herself and for her infant child, in the scorching heat searching for water, she is running around the House of Allah. Then she is seen running between Safa and Marwah; she is exhausted from thirst, worn out and tired, and fears for her child's life. When she returns for the seventh time, she is broken by despair. She sees before the beautiful child a spring of clear water gushing forth. This is the spring of Zamzam. In the desert of dryness and despair, it is a spring of the mercy of Allah.

Then the image of Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) appears in the imagination. He sees in a dream that he is slaughtering Hazrat Ismaʿil. He immediately prepares to sacrifice his beloved child. Without the slightest hesitation for a moment, he attains the lofty station of believing obedience.

*Qāla yā bunayya innī arā fī al-manāmi annī adhbaḥuka fa-unẓur māḏā tara* "He said, 'O my son, I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you; what do you think?'" Hazrat Ismaʿil (peace be upon him) also answers with great obedience:

*Yā abati if'al mā tu'mar, satajidunī in shā' Allāh min aṣ-ṣābirīn* "Father, do what you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient." When both of them are prepared, the mercy of Allah is stirred, and the ransom in exchange for this sacrifice is accepted.

*Wa-nādaynāhu an yā Ibrāhīm (103) qad ṣaddaqta al-ru'yā; innā kadhālika najzī al-muḥsinīn (105) inna hādhā lahuwa al-balā'u al-mubīn (106) wa-fadaynāhu bi-dhibḥin ʿaẓīm (108)* (37:103–108) "And We called out to him, 'O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision.' Thus do We reward the good-doers. Indeed, this was a clear trial. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice." And We freed that child by giving a great sacrifice as ransom.

Then Hazrat Ibrahim and Ismaʿil (peace be upon them both) are seen raising the foundations of the Kaʿbah, making supplication with great humility and submission.

*Rabbanā taqabbal minnā … ar-raḥīm (128)* "Our Lord, accept this service from us; You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. Our Lord, make us both Muslims to You, and from our offspring raise up a community that is Muslim to You, show us our rites of worship, and forgive our shortcomings. You are the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful."

These imagined images and personalities appear before and after on the screen of the imagination, and these memories come and go, when suddenly Hazrat ʿAbd al-Muttalib appears. He makes a vow: "O Allah, if You grant me ten sons, I will dedicate the tenth son to You." The tenth son is ʿAbdullah. ʿAbd al-Muttalib wishes to fulfil his vow, and his people gather around him, and they suggest that he give a ransom. He draws arrows beside the Kaʿbah, and each time the arrow for slaughtering ʿAbdullah comes out. They keep increasing the ransom until the ransom camels reach one hundred, although the initial standard of ransom was ten she-camels. At last the arrow of ransom came out. They sacrificed one hundred camels, and the life of ʿAbdullah was spared. This was the will of Allah, because Allah was to bring forth from his loins and the womb of Aminah the highly exalted Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Thus this ransom, the great ransom, was secured by Allah for the sake of Muhammad ﷺ.

After this, many memories are still associated with this House, and on the screen of imagination new personalities keep appearing. Hazrat Muhammad ﷺ is passing through the stages of childhood, and he is walking around the House of Allah. Look, you see him lifting the Black Stone with his blessed hands and placing it in its place, so as to end the strife which threatened to cause war among the tribes. You see him praying, you see him performing tawaf, you see him delivering sermons, you see him in seclusion (iʿtikaf). Your steps are on the screen of imagination. Your image lives in hearts. It is almost that a pilgrim sees you with his eyes while he is lost and absorbed in these memories. Then before us come the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ in droves, and they walk around on this earth, performing tawaf of the House of Allah. These scenes are such that it is almost as if the ears hear and the eyes see. And beyond these memories and imaginings, Hajj is a comprehensive global gathering of Muslims. In it they come to know their true reality and their root, which in history goes back far to Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

*Millata abīkum Ibrāhīm, huwa sammākumu al-muslimīna min qablu wa-fī hādhā* "The creed of your father Ibrahim. He named you Muslims before, and in this (Qur'an)." This is the axis around which they revolve, and which has united them. It is their symbol and their banner. Under it all gather; it is an ideological symbol and an ideological banner under whose shade people of all nations, all races, all colours and all languages come together. All distinctions are erased. Here, Muslims begin to feel this strength of theirs for a limited time: the strength of the belief in Tawhid, the strength of being one community, and the strength of unity and harmony among billions of Muslims. In this gathering they feel, for a limited time, the strength they had forgotten, and they feel it in such a way that if they become one, no power in the world can stand before them, provided all these people gather under one banner upon the belief in Tawhid.

As for what Allah says, *li-yashhadū manāfiʿa lahum* (22:28) "so that they may witness their benefits which have been made available for them": every generation, according to its circumstances, according to its needs and requirements, according to its experience and demands, can derive benefits from this gathering. Allah has placed this purpose in the gathering since the time He commanded Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to call people to visit this House.

The Qur'an gives certain rites and fundamental symbols for this gathering, and in all of them there is good for all.

*Wa-yadhkurū ismallāhi fī ayyāmin maʿlūmātin ʿalā mā razaqahum min bahīmati al-anʿām* (22:28) "And that they may mention the name of Allah on known days over the cattle He has provided for them." This verse points to the sacrifice that is performed on the day of Eid and during the days of tashriq, and various sacrificial animals are slaughtered. In mentioning sacrifice, the Qur'an first commands that the name of Allah be pronounced over it, because the purpose is the worship of Allah and the attainment of His good pleasure. Here, in the act of sacrifice, the most distinctive thing mentioned is that the name of Allah should be taken over it. The meaning is that the mere slaughtering of animals is not the goal, but the real aim is to mention the name of Allah over it. (The Hanafi ruling is that sacrifice is permissible only within the two days after the Day of Nahr.)

This sacrifice is a memorial of the great slaughter of Hazrat Ismaʿil (peace be upon him). It is also a memorial of one of the miracles of Allah and one of the great acts of obedience to the command of Allah, which Hazrat Ibrahim and Hazrat Ismaʿil (peace be upon them both) left as a memorial. The benefit in this memorial is that provision of food is made for the poor and needy. The sacrificial animals are camels, cows, buffaloes, sheep and goats. (For both cows and buffaloes the Arabic word *baqar* is used.)

*Fa-kulū minhā wa-aṭʿimū al-bāʾisa al-faqīr* (22:28) "So eat from it and feed the distressed poor." The command to the one who sacrifices to eat from the meat is recommended (mustahabb), but the command to give to the poor is obligatory (wājib). The command to eat from it is given so that the poor may feel that this is pure, clean and good meat.

As soon as the sacrifice is made, the pilgrim becomes permitted in those things which were forbidden to him during Hajj. For example, shaving the head, cutting hair, cutting nails, removing underarm hair, and bathing, and whatever was prohibited during the state of ihram becomes permissible. Regarding this it is said:

*Thumma liyaqḍū tafathahum wa-liyūfū nudhūrahum* (22:29) "Then let them end their untidiness and fulfil their vows." The vows they have made, that is, apart from the sacrifice of Hajj, the vows they have made.

*Wa-liyaṭṭawwafū bil-bayti al-ʿatīq* (22:29) "And let them circumambulate the ancient House." This refers to the ṭawāf al-iqāmah or ṭawāf al-ziyārah (whatever name is given). The ṭawāf al-iqāmah is separate from the ṭawāf al-widāʿ.

The "ancient House" refers to al-Masjid al-Ḥarām. Allah has protected it from the rule of any tyrant, and likewise has protected it from collapse and from its signs being effaced. Through the settlement of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) it has always remained inhabited and will always remain so.

This is the story of the construction of the Sacred House. And this is the fundamental belief upon which it was built: that Allah commanded Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to build it as a House of Tawhid and to keep it free from shirk and idol worship, and commanded him to direct the general public to visit it, to mention the name of Allah over the sacrificial animals, and not to mention the name of any other deity. To eat from the sacrificial meat oneself and also feed the destitute and the poor. This is the Sacred House, and in it the sanctities of Allah are preserved. These will be acted upon, and the first of Allah's sanctities is the Islamic worldview and the belief in Tawhid. The doors of this House should be open to all people, the lives and property of all people should be secure here, all covenants should be fulfilled here, and peace and security should be respected.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 22, verses 30–31:

[The Qur'anic quotation at the start, "ذلک ومن ……مکان سحیق (31)", is a fragment that spans verses 30–31; the passage is rendered below as it stands.]

That is so. And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah, it is better for him in the sight of his Lord. The necessary result of honouring the sacred things of Allah is that they are not even touched. This is a very great goodness and virtue with Allah. There is also abundant good in the world of human consciousness and the human conscience. There is good in practical, real life as well, because the conscience that is aware of what is sacred and strives to refrain from it is the one that will be pure. In a life where the sacred things of Allah are respected, that life can be filled with the blessing of peace, security and safety, and in it no one can be subjected to any oppression or injustice. In such a life, places of peace and homes of tranquillity can be found.

The polytheists too used to show reverence to certain animals, for example the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham. In their view these animals were sacred, and even touching them was a crime. But these were sanctities invented by the polytheists themselves; Allah had given no command concerning them. Therefore here it is said that the things Allah has made unlawful among the eating animals should be mentioned, for example carrion, blood, swine, and the animal that is dedicated to anyone other than Allah.

﴿Lawful for you are the cattle, except what is recited to you﴾ (22:30). This is so that no prohibition may be set by anyone other than Allah. No one is permitted to declare things lawful or unlawful except Allah, and no rulings may be enforced according to any law other than the Shari'ah of Allah.

In connection with the discussion of lawful and unlawful, the command to avoid the filth of idols was also emphasised. The polytheists used to slaughter animals on idols, although this was impurity. Rijs (filth, impurity) refers to that impurity which is connected with a person's self, conscience and mind; shirk is exactly this kind of spiritual impurity. Shirk defiles the heart and conscience in the same way that filth defiles a garment.

Then, shirk is a false attribution against Allah, and it is a blatant lie. Therefore Allah commands that, along with this great lie, one should keep away from all lies. ﴿So avoid the filth of idols, and avoid false speech﴾ (22:30). The Qur'an, by joining lying with shirk, has made its sin even more terrible. Imam Ahmad narrates that Qatadah al-Asadi reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed the morning prayer, then turned and stood up, and said:

"The testimony of falsehood has been made equal to associating partners with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

Then he recited this verse.

Allah desires that people abandon every form of shirk and every form of falsehood, and remain firmly upon pure monotheistic belief: ﴿Turning to Allah, not associating anything with Him﴾ (22:31). After this, the verse presents a frightening scene in the form of a parable: how is the state of one who falls from the lofty horizon of tawhid? He falls into the depths of shirk, and is so destroyed that not even his name or trace remains, as if he never existed.

﴿And whoever associates others with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky, and the birds snatch him away, or the wind throws him into a far-off place﴾ (22:31). Here "fallen from the sky" describes a person who falls from a very high place, so that as he falls from the sky he is shattered to pieces, birds snatch him away, or the wind casts him out of sight. Or the wind throws him into a pit where he finds no rest. In this scene, all the stages occur very rapidly: the swiftness, the successive actions, and the use of connectives that indicate events following one another without interval of time, meaning this person disappears from the scene very quickly. This is the distinctive style of the Qur'an in depicting imagery.

Just as the Qur'an has depicted the one who associates partners with Allah, so in reality his condition is much like this, for he falls from the lofty station of tawhid and faith, and his personality is scattered, because he no longer has the firm foundation, namely belief in the oneness of Allah, upon which he could stand. Now there is no place of settlement left for him. Birds will snatch him, meaning that base desires and superstitions and myths will pull him from every side. Since he has no strong rope in his hand, he will be dragged in every direction, falling sometimes to one side and sometimes to the other, because there is no firm foundation beneath his feet.

Now the discussion moves forward. The command is given to honour the sacred things of Allah and not to violate them. It is said: honour the symbols (sha'a'ir) of Allah. What are the sha'a'ir? They are the animals that are sacrificed during Hajj. Among the honouring of them is that they should be healthy, well-fed and valuable.

Within these symbols and rites are memories linked to Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and the periods after him, and their essential aim is obedience to Allah and turning towards Him. The animals whose sanctity is being discussed are slaughtered at the end of the days of ihram (the state of consecration for Hajj). If he needs them, he may ride them, and if he needs their milk, he may use it, until they reach their place of sacrifice, which is the Ancient House (al-Bayt al-'Atiq), that is, the Ka'bah. Rather, his intention was to sell it, buy more animals with that money, and slaughter them. He did not wish to sell it and buy more she-camels or cows. Although in that case there would have been more meat, from the perspective of consciousness and of giving good wealth in the way of Allah, this was weightier, and the value of conscious intention carries greater importance.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 22, verses 34–35:

ولکل امۃ ……ینفقون (35)

The policy of the Islamic system of life is that it connects a person's feelings and inclinations with the Being of Allah. Accordingly, its scheme is that consciousness, action, activity, worship, every movement and every habit should be given a new direction, and everything should be dyed in the color of Islam as a worldview (nazariya-i-hayat). From this perspective, Islam has declared forbidden those slaughtered animals over which a name other than Allah's has been pronounced at the time of slaughter, and it has made it obligatory that the slaughtered animals be over Allah's name, and indeed that "Allahu Akbar" be said in a loud voice at the very moment of slaughter. It is as if the animal is slaughtered precisely so that Allah's name may be pronounced in this way.

﴿And for every nation We have appointed a rite, that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them of livestock animals﴾ (22:34). "For every community We have appointed a rite of sacrifice, so that its people may pronounce the name of Allah over the animals He has bestowed upon them."

Then comes the explicit affirmation of the doctrine of Tawhid.

﴿So your God is one God﴾ (22:34). "(The purpose is only that) your God is one God." When God is one, obedience in every matter should also be to that one alone.

﴿So submit to Him﴾ (22:34). "Then become obedient to Him." This obedience is not obedience through compulsion, nor is there any compulsion in Islam; rather, the intention is to bow in submission with the willing consent of the heart.

﴿And give good tidings to the humble (mukhbitin)﴾ (22:34), ﴿who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾ (22:35). "O Prophet (ﷺ), give good news to those who adopt a humble manner, whose condition is that when they hear the mention of Allah, their hearts tremble." **Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah al-Hajj, verses 36–37:**

﴿وَالْبُدْنَ جَعَلْنَاهَا لَكُم مِّن شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ لَكُمْ فِيهَا خَيْرٌ ... وَبَشِّرِ الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (22:37)

Here, among the sacrificial animals, only the camel is mentioned, because it is the largest. Its being slaughtered in sacrifice is beneficial for you. It is beneficial while it is alive, since you ride on it and milk it, and when it is slaughtered you eat its meat. Therefore, when slaughtering this "good" (khayr), it is your duty to mention the name of Allah over it. Mention the name of Allah over it even when it is being prepared for slaughter, while they stand in a row.

﴿فَاذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهَا صَوَافَّ﴾ (22:36) "So mention the name of Allah over them while they are standing in rows."

Camels are slaughtered in such a way that they stand on three legs with one leg tied. When they fall after slaughter and their backs settle on the ground, then if you wish to eat from them, eat, and give their meat to the poor person who does not ask, and also give it to the one who asks. For this reason Allah has subjected them to you, so that people may thank God for this "good" (khayr) which is in them for people, both in life and after being slaughtered.

﴿كَذَٰلِكَ سَخَّرْنَاهَا لَكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ﴾ (22:36) "Thus We have subjected them to you, so that you may be grateful."

The command given to you, that you slaughter them mentioning the name of Allah, has the purpose: ﴿لَن يَنَالَ اللَّهَ لُحُومُهَا وَلَا دِمَاؤُهَا﴾ (22:38) "Neither their meat nor their blood reaches Allah." Blood and meat do not reach Allah, nor does He need them. What Allah desires is the attitude of fear of God. Therefore, this act of the polytheists of Makkah, who slaughtered animals, took the blood, and smeared it on idols, was merely a vulgar act. Allah is free of need for it.

﴿كَذَٰلِكَ سَخَّرَهَا لَكُمْ لِتُكَبِّرُوا اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَاكُمْ﴾ (22:37) "Thus He has subjected them to you, so that you may glorify Allah for having guided you."

He has guided you to the belief in the Oneness of God. He has guided you to turn towards Him, He has guided you to establish a true relationship between Allah and the servant, and He has guided you to give your deeds the right direction.

﴿وَبَشِّرِ الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾ (22:37) "And give good tidings to the good-doers." Those whose conception is beautiful, whose consciousness is beautiful, whose worship is also excellent, and whose connection with Allah is one of fear of God.

Thus every step of a Muslim, every movement of his, and every thought of his is such that he keeps the Divine Being in view in it. In it his heart is overflowing with fear of God, and in every matter he seeks the pleasure of Allah. In short, his whole life fulfills the purpose for which man was created, and in this world too his life is healthy and beneficial, and the branches of its ultimate goal are in the heavens.

These symbols (sha'a'ir) and rites (manasik) of Islam are fixed. Acts of worship and places of worship have been determined, and their respect has been declared necessary. Therefore there is a need for a power that establishes respect for these symbols, establishes the right of freedom of thought and vision, and creates opportunities for every person to worship Allah according to his belief. It should also keep intact the sanctity of places of worship. Further, it should make possible that believers, worshippers, and righteous people who perform good deeds can establish a system of life according to their view of life, which on one side is connected with Allah, Most High, and on the other side is a source of good and blessing for all humanity in this world. In short, it should be the guarantor of the welfare of this world and the Hereafter.

For this reason, after the Hijrah, Muslims were permitted to take up arms in the way of Allah, so that they could defend their community and defend their outlook and belief, and so that if any enemy attacked their territory, they could repel it, because oppression and persecution of Muslims had reached its limit. The sole purpose of this fighting (qital) is that freedom of beliefs and views, including for the people of Islam, may be established. Within the system of Allah's religion, the promise of Allah's help may take the form of reality, and they may be able to fulfill the obligations of the religion of Islam and the system of Islam, which are mentioned in the verses below.
